summary.text: Any witness below \(2^{2^k+1}\) must have totient exactly \(2^{2^k}\) and be odd; such an integer is squarefree with every prime factor a Fermat prime, and comparing totients expresses \(2^k\) as a sum of distinct powers of two, forcing \(F_k\) itself to be prime and to divide the witness. Thus \(F_k\), when prime, is the least witness, while if it is composite no witness lies below \(2^{2^k+1}\), which is itself a witness by the totient formula for powers of two; specialize to \(k=33\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
A(n)=\min\{m\ge 1:2^n\mid \varphi(m)\},
\]
where \(\varphi\) is Euler's totient function. The set over which the minimum is taken is nonempty: for every \(n\ge 0\),
\[
\varphi(2^{n+1})=2^n,
\]
so \(2^{n+1}\) is always an admissible value.

We shall prove the stronger statement that for every \(k\ge 0\), if
\[
F_k=2^{2^k}+1
\]
is the \(k\)-th Fermat number, then
\[
A(2^k)=
\begin{cases}
F_k,&\text{if }F_k\text{ is prime},\\[2mm]
2^{2^k+1},&\text{if }F_k\text{ is not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
Taking \(k=33\) gives the desired assertion.

We begin with several lemmas.

**1. An estimate for even integers.** If \(m\) is even, then
\[
2\varphi(m)\le m.
\]

We prove this by strong induction on \(m\). Write \(m=2r\). There is nothing to prove when \(r=0\). Suppose \(r>0\). If \(r\) is even, then the standard doubling formula for the totient gives
\[
\varphi(2r)=2\varphi(r).
\]
The induction hypothesis, applied to the smaller even integer \(r\), gives \(2\varphi(r)\le r\). Consequently
\[
2\varphi(2r)=4\varphi(r)\le 2r=m.
\]
If instead \(r\) is odd, then
\[
\varphi(2r)=\varphi(r).
\]
Since \(\varphi(r)\le r\), it follows that
\[
2\varphi(2r)=2\varphi(r)\le 2r=m.
\]
This proves the estimate.

**2. Structure of an odd integer whose totient is a power of two.** Suppose \(m\) is odd and
\[
\varphi(m)=2^n.
\]
Then every prime occurs in \(m\) with exponent exactly one, and every prime divisor of \(m\) is a Fermat number.

Indeed, let \(p\mid m\) be prime, and let \(r\ge 1\) be the exponent of \(p\) in the prime factorization of \(m\). Then \(p^r\mid m\). The elementary divisibility property of the totient says that if \(d\mid m\), then \(\varphi(d)\mid\varphi(m)\); this also follows immediately by comparing the prime-power formulas in the factorizations of \(d\) and \(m\). Thus
\[
\varphi(p^r)=p^{r-1}(p-1)\mid 2^n.
\]
If \(r\ge 2\), then \(p\mid 2^n\), so the prime \(p\) must equal \(2\). But \(m\) is odd, so this is impossible. Hence \(r=1\) for every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\). Thus \(m\) is squarefree and
\[
\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\mid m}(p-1),
\]
the product being over the distinct prime divisors of \(m\).

In particular, for each prime \(p\mid m\), the factor \(p-1\) divides \(2^n\), so
\[
p-1=2^e
\]
for some \(0\le e\le n\). Since \(m\) is odd, \(p\ne2\). Therefore \(p\) is odd, \(p-1>1\), and hence \(e>0\).

We now use the familiar elementary characterization of primes of the form \(2^e+1\): if \(2^e+1\) is prime, then \(e\) is a power of two. For completeness, write
\[
e=2^i u
\]
with \(u\) odd. If \(u>1\), put \(x=2^{2^i}>1\). Because \(u\) is odd,
\[
x^u+1=(x+1)(x^{u-1}-x^{u-2}+\cdots-x+1),
\]
and both factors are greater than one. This would make \(2^e+1=x^u+1\) composite. Thus \(u=1\), so \(e=2^i\). It follows that every prime divisor \(p\) of \(m\) has the form
\[
p=2^{2^i}+1=F_i
\]
for some \(i\ge0\).

**3. The Fermat factor forced by the exact totient.** We next prove that if \(m\) is odd and
\[
\varphi(m)=2^{2^k},
\]
then \(F_k\) is prime and \(F_k\mid m\).

By the preceding lemma, the distinct prime divisors of \(m\) can be written as \(F_i\)'s. Distinct prime divisors give distinct indices, because the Fermat numbers \(F_i=2^{2^i}+1\) are strictly increasing. Since \(m\) is squarefree,
\[
2^{2^k}=\varphi(m)=\prod_{p\mid m}(p-1)
 =\prod_{F_i\mid m}2^{2^i}
 =2^{\sum_{F_i\mid m}2^i}.
\]
Injectivity of the powers of \(2\) therefore gives
\[
\sum_{F_i\mid m}2^i=2^k. \tag{1}
\]
We claim that the index \(k\) must occur in this sum. First, every occurring index satisfies \(i\le k\), since its positive summand \(2^i\) is at most the whole sum \(2^k\). If \(k\) itself did not occur, all occurring indices would be distinct members of \(\{0,1,\ldots,k-1\}\). Their sum would then be at most
\[
1+2+\cdots+2^{k-1}=2^k-1,
\]
contrary to (1). Hence \(F_k\) is one of the prime divisors of \(m\). It follows simultaneously that \(F_k\) is prime and that \(F_k\mid m\).

**4. Any sufficiently small admissible number forces \(F_k\).** Suppose now that \(m>0\),
\[
2^{2^k}\mid\varphi(m),
\]
and
\[
m<2^{2^k+1}.
\]
We claim again that \(F_k\) is prime and divides \(m\).

Write
\[
\varphi(m)=c\,2^{2^k}
\]
for an integer \(c\ge0\). Since \(m>0\), its totient is positive, so \(c>0\). Also \(\varphi(m)\le m\), and hence
\[
c\,2^{2^k}=\varphi(m)\le m<2^{2^k+1}=2\cdot2^{2^k}.
\]
Thus \(c<2\). Since \(c\) is a positive integer, \(c=1\), and therefore
\[
\varphi(m)=2^{2^k}. \tag{2}
\]

Moreover, \(m\) must be odd. For if \(m\) were even, the estimate from part 1 and (2) would give
\[
2^{2^k+1}=2\varphi(m)\le m,
\]
contrary to the assumed strict inequality. We may therefore apply part 3 to (2), obtaining
\[
F_k\text{ is prime},\qquad F_k\mid m. \tag{3}
\]
This is the central small-witness lemma.

We now determine the minimum \(A(2^k)\).

**Case 1: \(F_k\) is prime.** Since
\[
F_k=2^{2^k}+1,
\]
we have
\[
\varphi(F_k)=F_k-1=2^{2^k}.
\]
Thus \(F_k\) is admissible for the definition of \(A(2^k)\), and so
\[
A(2^k)\le F_k.
\]
We show that no smaller positive integer is admissible. Suppose that \(m<F_k\), with \(m>0\) and \(2^{2^k}\mid\varphi(m)\). Since \(2^k\ge1\), we have \(2^{2^k}>1\), and consequently
\[
F_k=2^{2^k}+1<2\cdot2^{2^k}=2^{2^k+1}.
\]
Therefore \(m<2^{2^k+1}\), so the small-witness lemma applies and gives \(F_k\mid m\). Positivity of \(m\) then implies \(F_k\le m\), contradicting \(m<F_k\). Hence every admissible positive integer is at least \(F_k\), and
\[
A(2^k)=F_k.
\]

**Case 2: \(F_k\) is not prime.** The integer
\[
M=2^{2^k+1}
\]
is admissible, because the prime-power formula for the totient gives
\[
\varphi(M)=\varphi(2^{2^k+1})=2^{2^k}.
\]
Thus
\[
A(2^k)\le 2^{2^k+1}.
\]
If some admissible positive integer \(m\
) were smaller than \(2^{2^k+1}\), the small-witness lemma would imply that \(F_k\) is prime, contrary to the hypothesis of this case. Hence there is no smaller admissible integer, and
\[
A(2^k)=2^{2^k+1}.
\]

Combining the two cases proves, for every \(k\ge0\),
\[
A(2^k)=
\begin{cases}
F_k,&F_k\text{ prime},\\
2^{2^k+1},&F_k\text{ not prime}.
\end{cases}
\]
Finally set \(k=33\). Then \(N=2^{33}\) and
\[
F_{33}=2^{2^{33}}+1.
\]
Therefore
\[
A(2^{33})=
\begin{cases}
F_{33},&F_{33}\text{ is prime},\\
2^{2^{33}+1},&F_{33}\text{ is not prime},
\end{cases}
\]
which is exactly the conjectured value.
